title: Mason's seafood market: weighted average cost of goods sold and gross profit on crab legs, and whether to switch to FIFO
participant_role: Accountant for Mason's, a small local seafood market, calculating cost of goods sold and gross profit on crab legs
judge_role: Owner of Mason's who wants the results and advice on whether to change inventory valuation methods
scenario:
You to assume the role of an accountant for MASON'S, a small local seafood market. The owner (judge) wants you to calculate cost of goods sold and gross profit for crab legs.

You have been provided with the following data showing the sales and purchases of crab legs for the month of October. One pound of crab legs is represented as 1 unit. The seafood market uses the weighted average method of valuing inventory.

[Table of October crab leg activity: see exhibits]

You will meet with the owner (judge) to go over the results. The owner (judge) is wondering if the company should use a different method of valuing inventory and would like your advice. Before meeting with the owner (judge), you refer to the code for inventory in the Accounting Standards Codification shown below:

330-10-30-9 Cost for inventory purposes may be determined under any one of several assumptions as to the flow of cost factors, such as first-in first-out (FIFO), average, and last-in first-out (LIFO). The major objective in selecting a method should be to choose the one which, under the circumstances, most clearly reflects periodic income.

You must:
- Find the cost of goods sold for crab legs for the month of October.
- Find the gross profit made by the supermarket from crab legs in October.
- Decide if the seafood market should consider using a different method of valuing inventory. Explain why or why not.

You will present the information to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge's) office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented the information and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: How does product spoilage affect inventory?

solution.overview: A strong answer pools the 33 units available ($1,354 total cost) into a weighted average cost of $41.03 per pound, giving cost of goods sold of $492.36 for the 12 pounds sold and gross profit of $119.64 on $612 of sales. It then explains that weighted average smooths cost swings, but because seafood spoils the physical flow is first-in first-out, so switching to FIFO would match recorded costs to the actual flow and show the most recent prices in ending inventory.

by_task.task: Cost of goods sold, weighted average
answer: Goods available: 5 x $46 = $230; 20 x $39 = $780; 8 x $43 = $344; total 33 units costing $1,354
Weighted average cost = $1,354 / 33 = $41.03 per pound
COGS = 12 units sold x $41.03 = $492.36
Ending inventory = 21 units x $41.03 = about $861.64 (total cost 1,354 minus 492.36)
Gross profit = $612.00 minus COGS $492.36 = $119.64
Gross margin = 119.64 / 612 = about 19.5%
Journal entries under a perpetual system: debit Cash or A/R 612, credit Sales 612; debit COGS 492.36, credit Inventory 492.36
Weighted average is good at smoothing out large swings in cost, like the $39 to $46 range here
Crab legs spoil, so the real physical flow is first-in first-out: sell the oldest pounds first to avoid losses
If the owner wants recorded COGS to follow the actual flow of the product, switch to FIFO
FIFO also leaves ending inventory on the balance sheet at the most recent prices rather than older ones
ASC 330-10-30-9 says to pick the method that most clearly reflects periodic income; for a perishable seller that points to FIFO
Comparison for October: FIFO COGS = 5 x 46 + 7 x 39 = $503 (gross profit $109); LIFO COGS = 8 x 43 + 4 x 39 = $500 (gross profit $112); weighted average $492.36 (gross profit $119.64)

Oct. 12 cost of the 12 pounds sold at weighted average $41.03

FIFO and LIFO comparison (model answer, not in PDF)
steps: FIFO: 5 x $46 + 7 x $39 = $230 + $273 = $503 COGS; gross profit $612 minus $503 = $109
LIFO: 8 x $43 + 4 x $39 = $344 + $156 = $500 COGS; gross profit $612 minus $500 = $112
calculations.result: Weighted average gives the highest October gross profit ($119.64) because the oldest units were the most expensive

judge_question_answers.question: How does product spoilage affect inventory?
answer: Spoiled product can no longer be sold, so it must be written off: debit a Spoilage or Inventory Loss expense, credit Inventory
It lowers the ending inventory value and raises expenses, cutting gross profit
Spoilage risk is why perishable sellers physically rotate stock first-in first-out and keep inventory levels low
Regular physical counts catch spoilage so the books match what is actually in the case

judge_question_answers.question: In a seafood market, should all perishable products use the same inventory method?
answer: Consistency matters: using one method for similar products makes statements comparable and easier for the owner and lenders to read
GAAP allows different methods for different classes of inventory, but the method chosen must be applied consistently period to period
For a small market, FIFO for all perishable seafood is simplest and matches how every perishable item actually moves
Non-perishable items (canned goods, supplies) could reasonably use a different method if it better reflects income

key_concepts.definition: Inventory costing method that averages the cost of all units available. Average cost per unit = Total cost of goods available / Total units available; COGS = Units sold x Average cost.
Assumes the oldest units are sold first, so COGS uses the earliest costs and ending inventory holds the most recent costs. Matches the physical flow of perishable goods.
Assumes the newest units are sold first, so COGS uses the latest costs. In rising-price periods it gives the highest COGS and lowest profit.

key_concepts.term: Cost of goods available for sale
key_concepts.definition: Beginning inventory + Purchases. Here $230 + $780 + $344 = $1,354 for 33 units.
The cost assigned to the units actually sold during the period. Cost of goods available minus ending inventory, or units sold x cost per unit.
Sales revenue minus cost of goods sold. Gross profit margin = Gross profit / Sales.
Units still on hand at period end times their assigned cost; it appears as a current asset on the balance sheet.
Inventory and COGS are updated at the time of each purchase and sale, so a sale needs two entries: one for revenue and one moving cost from Inventory to COGS.
The Accounting Standards Codification topic on inventory. Paragraph 330-10-30-9 allows FIFO, average or LIFO and says to choose the method that most clearly reflects periodic income.
Once a business picks an inventory method it should keep using it from period to period so results are comparable; changes must be justified and disclosed.
Removing spoiled or unsellable goods from inventory: debit Spoilage (or Inventory Loss) Expense, credit Inventory.

notes: The PDF SOLUTION shows the weighted average table (average $41.03, COGS $492.36), the gross profit computation ($119.64) and a paragraph recommending FIFO for perishable goods. It does not answer the two judge questions; those are model answers. The PDF solution states that in periods of rising prices FIFO creates a larger profit; that is true in general, but in this specific October data the beginning inventory ($46) was the most expensive lot, so FIFO would actually give a lower gross profit ($109) than weighted average ($119.64). The scenario text calls the business both a seafood market and a supermarket, and the first sentence reads 'You to assume the role' (missing 'are') in the original.
